activities.title: Arrange flowers together
activities.summary: Choose, trim and place flowers or leafy stems in a jar or vase together.
steps: Spread the towel on the table and lay the stems out side by side.
Fill the jar about halfway with water together.
Look at the stems together and ask which one they would like to start with.
Trim the end of that stem so it fits the jar. The helper can do the cutting.
Place the first stem in the jar, or hand it over so they can place it.
Take turns choosing and adding stems. There is no right shape.
Turn the jar around and look at it from each side together.
Agree on where the flowers should go, such as a windowsill or the table.
plainSteps: Spread the towel on the table.
Lay the stems out side by side.
Fill the jar about halfway with water.
Ask which stem they would like to start with.
Trim the end of that stem to fit the jar.
Let the helper do the cutting.
Place the first stem in the jar, or hand it over.
Take turns choosing and adding stems.
There is no right shape.
Turn the jar and look at each side.
Agree on where to put them, like a windowsill.
materials: A small bunch of flowers or leafy stems, checked as safe to handle
A jar, mug or vase that will not tip easily
Water in a jug
Scissors or pruners for the helper
An old towel or newspaper for the table
safety: Some common flowers and plants, such as lily of the valley, foxglove and daffodils, are toxic if eaten. Check every plant before use.
Lilies shed pollen that stains and can irritate skin; remove the pollen tips or choose other flowers.
Remove thorns and prickly leaves from roses and holly before handing stems over.
Keep scissors and pruners with the helper, and wipe up spilled water so nobody slips.
Supervise closely if petals or leaves might be put in the mouth.
activities.stopNote: It is fine to stop after one or two stems. A single flower in a jar is a finished arrangement. Put it somewhere it can be seen and enjoyed.

variations.text: Trim all the stems to the same length before you start and offer two at a time to choose from.
Use a small, heavy mug on a tray table with three to five short stems. Keep the water low to limit spills.
Choose large flowers in strong colors, such as yellow or orange, and use a plain dark jar for contrast.
Pick unscented flowers or plain green leaves, and work in a quiet spot with only a few stems out.
Give each person one stem to add to a shared vase, then talk about the finished arrangement together.
A child carries the stems and holds the vase steady while the grandparent chooses each flower and where it goes. Cutting stays with an adult.

activities.title: Decorate a keepsake box
activities.summary: Cover a shoebox with paper or fabric, then choose a few small things to keep inside.
steps: Set the box on the table with the lid off, and lay out the paper, the glue and the small items.
Choose the paper or fabric together. Any choice is fine.
Lay the paper on one side of the box, and ask the helper to trim it to a little larger than that side.
Glue the back of the paper and press it onto the side of the box, then fold the extra paper over the edges and smooth it flat with the hand.
Turn the box and repeat on each side, then cover the lid the same way.
Set the box aside for a few minutes so the glue holds.
Look through the small items together and choose a few to keep inside.
Place the chosen items in the box and put the lid on.
Agree on a place to keep the box, such as a shelf or the bedside table.

Press it onto the side of the box.

Put the lid on.

materials: An empty shoebox or small cardboard box with a lid
Wrapping paper, wallpaper scraps or light fabric, cut a little larger than each side of the box
A glue stick or double-sided tape
Scissors for the helper
A few small items chosen by the person, such as a ribbon, a shell or a copy of a photo
safety: Scissors are for the helper only, and keep the glue away from the mouth.
Use a glue stick or double-sided tape rather than spray glue.
Choose items too large to swallow, and leave out pins, buttons or anything sharp.
Use copies of photos or papers, and keep the originals somewhere safe.
activities.stopNote: It is fine to stop after one side. Put the box and its paper aside, and carry on another day, or simply enjoy a few of the items together.

variations.text: Start with a box that is already covered or painted, and add only a ribbon and a few small items.
Use a small box on a lap tray and cover only one side, with the items chosen to go on top.
Choose bold, high-contrast paper, and place the items where they are easy to see.
Use one large sheet of paper to wrap the whole box, so there are fewer pieces to handle.
Two or three people each decorate one side of the same box.
A child smooths the paper onto each side while the grandparent chooses the paper and the things to keep inside, and says why each one matters.

activities.title: Decorate a plant pot
activities.summary: A plain pot decorated with paint, paper or twine, ready for a plant or herb to live in.
steps: Cover the table and put the pot and materials within reach.
Offer two ways to decorate, such as paint or wrapped twine, and let them choose.
Paint the outside of the pot, or wrap twine around it while you hold the end in place.
Leave paint to dry for about an hour; twine is ready straight away.
Smell the plant or herb together and talk about where it might sit.
Spoon soil into the pot and set the plant in it, taking turns if that suits you both.
Water it lightly and put it on a windowsill or table where you can both see it.
plainSteps: Cover the table.
Put the pot and materials within reach.
Offer two ways to decorate, such as paint or wrapped twine.
Let them choose.
Paint the outside of the pot, or wrap twine around it.
Hold the end of the twine in place while you wrap.
Leave the paint to dry for about an hour.
Twine is ready straight away.
Smell the plant or herb together.
Talk about where it might sit.
Spoon soil into the pot.
Set the plant in it, taking turns if that suits you both.
Water it lightly.
Put it on a windowsill or table where you can both see it.
materials: A small terracotta or plastic plant pot
Non-toxic, water-based paint and a thick-handled brush
Garden twine or yarn (optional)
Paper napkins or magazine pictures with a glue stick (optional)
Newspaper to cover the table
A small plant, herb or bulb, and a little potting soil
safety: Use non-toxic, water-based paint, and wash it off skin with soap and water.
Wear gloves or wash hands after handling potting soil, and keep it away from mouths.
Choose plants that are safe to touch and not harmful if nibbled, such as basil, mint or parsley.
Check food cans for sharp rims before use, and tape over any rough edge.
activities.stopNote: It is fine to stop once the pot is painted. Let it dry and plant it another day, or use it as it is for pens, buttons or dried flowers.

variations.text: Paint a base coat in advance and offer one color for stripes or dots, or a ready-cut strip of paper to glue on.
Skip the soil and paint, and wrap the pot in soft yarn while it sits on a clean tray.
Decorate a small plastic pot on a lap tray with twine or a glue stick, and pot the plant later at a table.
A child paints the pot while the older adult chooses the plant and shows how to firm the soil.
Each person decorates a pot and the group plants a row of herbs to share on a common windowsill.
Paint with a sponge or a wide foam brush held in the whole hand, or wrap the twine around the pot while the helper holds the end in place.

activities.title: Draw a comic strip together
activities.summary: Take turns drawing three or four boxes of a comic strip about something ordinary, such as the cat or breakfast.
steps: Fold or draw lines to make three or four boxes on one sheet, in a row or a grid.
Choose something ordinary to draw about together, such as the cat, breakfast or the walk to the shop.
Say in one short line what happens in each box. Keep it simple, and let the other person change it if they like.
One person draws the first box while the other says what is in it. Stick figures and simple shapes are fine.
Swap, so the other person draws the next box.
Add a few words in a speech bubble if you like, written by whoever is holding the pencil.
Draw the last box together, with an ending that is funny or quiet, whichever you prefer.
Read the strip out loud, then put it where you can both see it. Stop here, or start a second strip.
plainSteps: Fold or draw lines to make three or four boxes.
Choose something ordinary to draw about together.
Say in one short line what happens in each box.
Let the other person change it if they like.
One person draws the first box.
The other person says what goes in it.
Stick figures and simple shapes are fine.
Swap, so the other person draws the next box.
Add a few words in a speech bubble if you like.
Whoever holds the pencil writes the words.
Draw the last box together.
Make the ending funny or quiet, whichever you prefer.
Read the strip out loud.
Put it where you can both see it.
Stop here, or start a second strip.
materials: Plain paper, one sheet for each strip
Pencils
Markers or crayons, washable if possible
A ruler, optional
A clipboard or tray to rest the paper on, optional
safety: Use washable markers if you can, and keep ink off skin that is sensitive.
Keep pencils and markers away from the mouth if anyone may chew or taste things.
Stay close, so the pencil and the paper are always easy to reach.
activities.stopNote: It is fine to stop after one box. Keep what is drawn, or add the next box another day. A strip with only one box is still a finished picture.

variations.text: Make just three boxes and agree on the whole plan first. One person draws every box while the other chooses what goes in them.
Rest the paper on a clipboard or lap tray, so no one needs to lean over a table.
The older adult is the writer: they decide what happens in each box and write the speech bubbles. The child draws what they say. Swap for the last box.
Hold up two simple drawings of the next box and let them point to the one they like. Draw it together.
Use a thick marker or a crayon with a foam grip, and make the boxes big, with only a few large shapes in each.

activities.title: Draw a map of a favorite place
activities.summary: Draw a simple map together of a place they know well or like, and talk about it as it grows.
steps: Sit side by side with the paper between you and the pens within reach.
Ask whether there is a place they would like to draw, such as a street, a garden, a kitchen or a beach.
Make the first mark together, such as a line for a road or a shape for a house. Any mark will do.
Ask what comes next, and draw it or hand them the pen. Any answer is the right one.
Add one thing at a time, and let them talk or stay quiet as they choose.
Do not correct what they draw or say. Do not ask for dates or names.
Stop when it feels finished, or when they have had enough, and agree where to put the map.
plainSteps: Sit side by side with the paper between you.
Keep the pens within reach.
Ask whether there is a place they would like to draw.
It could be a street, a garden, a kitchen or a beach.
Make the first mark together, such as a line for a road.
Any mark will do.
Ask what comes next.
Draw it, or hand them the pen.
Any answer is the right one.
Add one thing at a time.
Let them talk or stay quiet as they choose.
Do not correct what they draw or say.
Do not ask for dates or names.
Stop when it feels finished, or when they have had enough.
Agree where to put the map.
materials: A large sheet of plain paper
A thick marker, or pencils or crayons
A firm board or tray to rest on, if working in a chair or bed
safety: A place can bring back strong feelings. Listen kindly and let them lead. Offer to put the pen down, or move on to something lighter.
Never use the map to test them. Do not correct details or ask for dates, names or what happened.
Keep the helper nearby and offer to draw. They do not need to be good at drawing, and neither do you.
If a memory seems to upset them, stop drawing, sit with them and offer a drink or a change of scene.
activities.stopNote: It is fine to stop after one line. Put the map somewhere safe and carry on another day, or simply talk about the place for a while, or about something else.

variations.text: The helper draws everything the person points to or describes, and they choose where things go. Offer two choices at a time, such as a tree or a gate.
Use a lap tray or a firm board and a smaller sheet of paper. The helper holds the paper still and draws if asked.
Use a thick black marker on white paper, and keep the shapes large and few. Say aloud what you are drawing as you go.
Use a chunky marker, or wrap a regular pen in a rolled cloth to make it easier to hold. The helper steadies the paper.
The helper draws and points to a spot on the map. They answer by nodding, pointing or taking the pen to make a mark.
A grandchild draws what the older adult points to and talks about, and adds a small picture of their own beside it if they like.

activities.title: Draw a slow line pattern
activities.summary: Trace a circle round a cup, split it into sections and fill each with slow, repeating lines.
steps: Set the paper in front of the person and choose a pencil or marker together.
Hold the cup steady on the paper while they trace round its rim to make a circle.
Draw three or four curved or straight lines across the circle to split it into sections.
Pick one section and fill it with a slow repeat, such as short lines all leaning one way.
Move to the next section and try a different repeat, such as small circles, dots or zigzags.
Go one section at a time, resting the pencil between sections if you like.
Stop when the circle is full or whenever they want to, then turn the page around and look at it together.

Choose a pencil or marker together.
Hold the cup steady on the paper.
They trace round its rim to make a circle.
Draw three or four curved or straight lines across the circle.
This splits the circle into sections.
Pick one section.
Fill it with a slow repeat, such as short lines all leaning one way.
Move to the next section.
Try a different repeat, such as small circles, dots or zigzags.
Go one section at a time.
Rest the pencil between sections if you like.
Stop when the circle is full, or whenever they want to.
Turn the page around and look at it together.
materials: A sheet of plain paper
A cup or small bowl with a round rim, to trace round
A soft pencil or a thick marker
A second pen in another color, if wanted
safety: Use washable, non-toxic markers or crayons and keep them away from the mouth.
Put the caps back on markers when not in use, since they dry out and can stain skin.
Choose a pencil with a blunt, soft tip, and keep the tip pointing away from the face.
activities.stopNote: It is fine to stop after one section. Put the page aside and look at it later, or simply watch the lines being drawn without adding any.

variations.text: Trace the circle for them and draw only one dividing line. Fill the two halves with the same simple repeat, such as lines.
Work on a lap tray or a clipboard, with a non-slip mat under the paper so it stays still without a second hand.
Use a clipboard on a lap tray, a small circle traced from a saucer and just three sections.
Use a thick black marker on white paper and a large circle. Say each new shape aloud as it is drawn.
Use a jumbo crayon or a thick marker, or push a pencil through a foam ball so it is easy to hold in a loose fist.
A child holds the cup steady and traces the circle, then the older adult chooses the repeat for each section and a child copies it in another circle.

activities.title: Draw repeating patterns
activities.summary: Fill boxes on a page with simple repeating lines, loops and dots.
steps: Place the paper on the table, with the grid of boxes facing the person.
Choose a pencil or marker together, and offer a choice of color if they want one.
Make a short line or a dot in the first box, and invite them to copy it or add their own.
Fill the box with a simple repeat, such as lines going the same way or loops in a row.
Move to the next box and try a different repeat, such as dots, zigzags or circles.
Keep going one box at a time for as long as it feels pleasant.
Stop when the page is full or when they want to stop, then look at the pattern together.
plainSteps: Place the paper on the table, with the boxes facing the person.
Choose a pencil or marker together.
Offer a choice of color if they want one.
Make a short line or a dot in the first box.
Invite them to copy it or add their own.
Fill the box with a simple repeat.
For example, lines going the same way, or loops in a row.
Move to the next box.
Try a different repeat, such as dots, zigzags or circles.
Work one box at a time.
Keep going for as long as it feels pleasant.
Stop when the page is full, or when they want to stop.
Look at the pattern together.
materials: A sheet of plain paper, with a grid of large boxes drawn on it
A soft pencil, a thick marker or a crayon
A ruler, if the boxes need to be drawn
safety: Use washable, non-toxic markers or crayons, and keep them away from the mouth.
Put the caps back on markers when not in use, since they dry out and can stain skin.
If a ruler is used, choose one with a rounded edge, or none at all.
activities.stopNote: It is fine to stop after one box or a few lines. Put the page aside and look at it together later, or simply watch the marks being made without adding more.

variations.text: Draw one line for them to copy, then fill only the first row of boxes together.
Use a clipboard on a lap tray and a page with just four large boxes.
Use a thick black marker and large boxes with dark outlines, and say each line aloud as it is drawn.
Use one color and a slow, quiet pace, and stop whenever it feels like too much.
Offer to guide their hand gently, only if they seem comfortable with that, and pause often to see if they want to continue.
Use a jumbo crayon or a thick marker, or wrap a regular pencil in a foam hair curler so it is easy to hold in a loose fist.

activities.title: Draw to music
activities.summary: Listen to music together and let lines, shapes and colors follow the sound.
steps: Tape a sheet of paper to the table so it does not slide.
Lay out the crayons or markers and offer a choice of color.
Play the first piece of music at a comfortable volume.
Draw lines or shapes together that follow the music, fast or slow, big or small.
Swap colors whenever either of you likes.
Stop the music and look at the drawing together. Talk about it only if they want to.
Try a different piece of music on a new sheet, or stop there.
plainSteps: Tape a sheet of paper to the table so it does not slide.
Lay out the crayons or markers.
Offer a choice of color.
Play the first piece of music at a comfortable volume.
Draw lines or shapes together that follow the music.
Make them fast or slow, big or small.
Swap colors whenever either of you likes.
Stop the music.
Look at the drawing together.
Talk about it only if they want to.
Try a different piece of music on a new sheet.

materials: Large sheets of plain paper
Crayons, colored pencils or washable markers
A phone, radio or music player
A short list of three or four pieces of music with different moods
Masking tape to hold the paper still
safety: Keep the volume comfortable and check hearing aids are in and switched on. Avoid sudden loud music.
Use washable, non-toxic markers or crayons. Marker on skin usually washes off with soap and water; avoid drawing on skin.
Keep pens and crayons away from the mouth if the person may chew or taste things.
Some music brings up strong feelings. If they seem upset, pause, offer comfort, and switch to something calm.
activities.stopNote: It is fine to stop after a few marks or a single song. Keep listening together without drawing, or put the music on for a quiet moment instead.

variations.text: Use one chunky crayon and one slow piece of music. Simply moving the crayon back and forth is a full way to take part.
Tape the paper to a clipboard or lap tray and play music quietly from a phone close by.
Use thick black or dark markers on white paper, and describe aloud the shapes you are drawing.
Choose soft, steady music at low volume, one color and a small sheet. Stop if it feels like too much.
Take turns choosing the music. A child and an older adult draw on the same sheet from opposite sides.
Draw on one shared sheet. One person draws while the music plays, the other adds color when it pauses.

activities.title: Draw with oil pastels on dark paper
activities.summary: Draw simple shapes, a sky or a flower in bright oil pastels on black or dark paper.
steps: Spread newspaper over the table and rest the dark paper on a clipboard or flat board.
Open the pastels and set out a few bright colors where they are easy to reach.
Ask which color they would like to start with. Any choice is fine.
Draw a shape or a line on the dark paper, pressing firmly so the color shows clearly.
Add one thing at a time: a sky of colored bands, a sun, a flower, or just lines.
Lay a second color over the first if they like. The colors will blend together.
Wipe fingers on a paper towel when the pastel gets onto them.
Stop when they put the pastel down, then look at the picture together and choose where to put it.
plainSteps: Spread newspaper over the table.
Rest the dark paper on a clipboard or flat board.
Open the pastels.
Set out a few bright colors where they are easy to reach.
Ask which color they would like to start with.
Any choice is fine.
Draw a shape or a line on the dark paper.
Press firmly so the color shows clearly.
Add one thing at a time, such as a sky, a sun or lines.
Lay a second color over the first if they like.
The colors will blend together.

Stop when they put the pastel down.
Look at the drawing together.
Choose where to put it.
materials: Oil pastels in bright colors, a box of 12 or more
Black or dark blue construction paper
A clipboard or flat board to rest the paper on
Newspaper or an old cloth to cover the table
Paper towels or baby wipes for fingers
safety: Oil pastels are waxy and can stain skin, clothes and furniture, so cover the table and wipe fingers as you go.
Oil pastels are not food. Keep them away from the mouth if anyone may chew or taste things.
Pick up broken bits and crumbs from the floor so no one treads on them.
activities.stopNote: It is fine to stop after one mark. Put the pastels away, or leave the page out and add to it another day. One bold line is already a picture.

variations.text: Offer only three colors and ask for one big shape or a few long lines. A single bold shape is a complete picture.
Use black paper with white, yellow and light pastels, and draw large, thick shapes under good light. Describe each color out loud as it goes on.
Use chunky oil pastels, or slip a short pastel into a foam tube, and hold it in the whole hand. Draw big sweeping marks with the whole arm.
Rest the board on a lap tray with a few pastels in a shallow box beside it, so everything is within reach.
A child picks the next color and the older adult chooses where it goes on the page, then swap. Each person can also take one half of the sheet.

activities.title: Fold a paper boat
activities.summary: A classic folded paper boat made from a single sheet, which you can float together in a basin of water.
steps: Fold the sheet in half from top to bottom and run a thumbnail along the crease.
Fold the two top corners down to the middle to make a triangle.
Fold the bottom strip up on each side, over the triangle.
Open the shape from the bottom and press it flat into a diamond.
Fold the bottom point of the diamond up to the top, on each side, to make a small triangle.
Open it again from the bottom and press it flat into a smaller diamond.
Gently pull the two top points apart, and the boat will open out.
Float it together in a basin of water, or set it on a shelf to keep.
plainSteps: Fold the sheet in half from top to bottom.
Run a thumbnail along the crease.
Fold the two top corners down to the middle.
Fold the bottom strip up over the triangle.
Do the same on the other side.
Open the shape from the bottom.
Press it flat into a diamond.
Fold the bottom point up to the top.
Do the same on the other side, to make a small triangle.
Open it again from the bottom.
Press it flat into a smaller diamond.
Gently pull the two top points apart.
Float the boat in a basin of water.
Or set it on a shelf to keep.
materials: A rectangular sheet of paper, such as printer paper or newspaper
A flat, clear table
A wide basin or tray of shallow water (optional)
A towel for drying hands
safety: Use only a few inches of water in a basin or tray, and stay with anyone near water.
Mop up spills straight away so the floor does not become slippery.
Paper edges can give small cuts; fold with the flat of the hand if skin is fragile.
activities.stopNote: It is fine to stop halfway. A folded triangle is a paper hat, which is a fine result on its own, and you can finish the boat another day or not at all.

variations.text: Fold the first few steps in advance and invite them to do the last pull that opens the boat out.
Fold two boats side by side, one step at a time, copying each other's folds.
The older adult shows the folds while a child follows, then everyone races the boats in a basin.
Use a large sheet of brightly colored paper on a dark table, and guide hands to each fold if they welcome it.
Each person folds or decorates a boat, and the group floats them together in a wide tray of water.
Crease each fold ahead of time, or press each one flat with a ruler or the side of a hand instead of pinching the paper.

activities.title: Fold towels together
activities.summary: Fold warm towels from the dryer together and stack them, with no wrong way to fold.
steps: Sit at a table, or stand at a counter, with the basket of towels beside you.
Lift one towel from the basket and shake it out once.
Bring one edge across to meet the opposite edge.
Smooth the towel flat with both hands.
Fold it in half, or in thirds, however they like.
Place the folded towel on the pile.
Repeat with the next towel, and swap jobs whenever they like.
Stack the finished towels in the laundry basket or cupboard.
plainSteps: Sit at a table, or stand at a counter.
Keep the basket of towels beside you.
Lift one towel and shake it out once.
Bring one edge across to meet the opposite edge.
Smooth the towel flat with both hands.
Fold it in half or in thirds, however they like.
Place the folded towel on the pile.
Repeat with the next towel.
Swap jobs whenever they like.
Stack the finished towels in the laundry basket or cupboard.
materials: A basket of clean, dry towels, warm from the dryer
A large flat table, counter or bed to fold on
A laundry basket or cupboard for the finished pile
safety: Check towels are warm, not hot, before handing them over. Test with the inside of your wrist first.
Before folding, check each towel for pins, loose buttons or other small items that could be dropped or swallowed.
If standing, keep the floor clear of dropped towels and pets, and keep a chair close so they can sit whenever they like.
Keep towels away from stove burners, space heaters and open flames.
Stay with the person while they fold, and remove any pin or button before it can be dropped or swallowed.
activities.stopNote: It is fine to stop after one towel. Leave the rest in the basket, or stack what is folded and sit together for a while.

variations.text: The helper does the first fold, and the person smooths each towel flat and places it on the pile.
Sit at a table for the whole task, folding towels on a low table with the basket beside you.
Use towels at room temperature instead of warm ones, or choose plain cotton without loops if rough fabric is uncomfortable.
Two people hold opposite corners of each towel and fold it together, one towel at a time.
Use small hand towels or a bath towel that is easy to lift in both hands, and fold on a table at elbow height. Smooth and fold with the flat palms instead of pinching the corners.

activities.title: Give a hand massage
activities.summary: Gently massage one hand with a little plain lotion, asking first and stopping whenever they wish.
steps: Wash and dry your hands, then sit beside them with the lotion and towel in reach.
Ask if they would like a hand massage, and wait for a clear yes.
Ask which hand they would like to start with, and rest it on the towel.
Warm a small drop of lotion between your palms.
Rest your hands lightly around theirs, without gripping.
Stroke slowly from the wrist toward the knuckles, on the back of the hand.
Move to each finger in turn, with light, slow pressure.
Ask how it feels, and stop straight away if they pull away.
Wipe any extra lotion with the towel, and let the hand rest.
plainSteps: Wash and dry your hands.
Sit beside them with the lotion and towel in reach.
Ask if they would like a hand massage.
Wait for a clear yes.
Ask which hand they would like to start with.
Rest that hand on the towel.
Warm a small drop of lotion between your palms.
Rest your hands lightly around theirs, without gripping.
Stroke slowly from the wrist toward the knuckles, on the back of the hand.
Move to each finger in turn, with light, slow pressure.
Ask how it feels.
Stop straight away if they pull away.
Wipe any extra lotion with the towel.
Let the hand rest.
materials: A small bottle of plain, unscented lotion or hand cream
A clean, soft towel to rest the hand on
A chair with arms, or a pillow to support the arm
A bowl of warm water and a towel for washing hands first (optional)
safety: Ask permission before touching, and stop as soon as they pull away, tense up or say to stop.
Test a small drop of plain lotion on the inside of the wrist first, and check for known allergies or skin reactions.
Do not press on red, swollen, bruised, broken or very thin skin. A dry, gentle wipe is enough there.
Avoid sore joints, and never bend fingers past the point where they move easily.
activities.stopNote: It is fine to stop after one hand, or even one finger. Wipe the hand dry, rest it on the towel, and sit quietly together.

variations.text: Hold the hand in both of yours and make a few slow strokes on the back of it, or simply hold it for a moment.
Sit on the edge of the bed or on a chair beside it, with the hand resting on a pillow. Keep the session to a few minutes.
Skip the lotion and use dry hands with very light touch, or wrap a warm towel around the hand instead.
Offer an open palm and wait for the hand to come toward you. Stop if it pulls away or the face looks uneasy.
Rest the hand on a rolled towel so the fingers stay open without effort. Stroke with the whole palm, and move each finger only as far as it moves easily.

activities.title: Hold a sing-along at home
activities.summary: Play or sing a few songs they choose, and join in however they like: singing, humming, clapping or just listening.
steps: Sit together somewhere comfortable, with the music player within reach.
Ask what kind of music they would like today, or offer two choices.
Play the first tune, or start humming one they name, at a comfortable volume.
Join in however they like: sing, hum, clap, sway or just listen.
Let the tune finish. Do not fill the quiet, and do not ask anyone to sing a particular part.
Ask whether they would like another, and choose it together.
Stop after a few tunes, or sooner if they have had enough.

A comfortable seat for each person
A speaker, if you have one
safety: Set the volume low and check it with them. Sudden loud sound can startle or hurt.

No one is tested on the words. Never ask for a missing line or correct a wrong one.
If a tune seems to upset them, change it or stop. Their choice comes first.
activities.stopNote: It is fine to stop after one tune. Turn the music off, sit quietly together, or offer a cup of tea. Try again another day if they would like.

variations.text: Offer just two tunes at a time and play only one or two. Listening, tapping a hand or a smile is a full way to take part.
Sit beside the bed at a low volume, with the phone close but not on the bed. Hum along softly, or just listen together.
Everyone stays in their chairs. Clap, tap a knee or sway gently to the beat, as much or as little as they like.
Take turns choosing the next tune. Anyone may pass. Keep the volume low enough that everyone can hear each other talk between tunes.
Play two short tunes and watch where their eyes, hands or feet go. Tapping, smiling or leaning in is an answer.
The older adult picks a tune they like and the child picks the next one. Either can clap, hum or simply listen, and both can say pass.

activities.title: Look through a photo album
activities.summary: Turn the pages of a family photo album together, pausing to talk about what is in each picture.
steps: Sit side by side at a table, or with a lap tray, with the album in easy reach.
Check that glasses are on and the light is bright enough to see the pictures clearly.
Let them open the album to any page they like.
Ask an open question, such as "What can you see here?" or "Tell me about this one."
Listen to what they say, and accept it without checking or correcting it.
Turn the page only when they are ready, or ask whether they would like to turn it.
If a picture brings up sadness, pause, offer a tissue and sit quietly together.
Close the album gently when they are ready, and rest your hand on the cover.

Reading glasses, a magnifier or a lamp, if they help
safety: Some photos bring up sadness or loss. Keep tissues close and do not push a conversation that is upsetting them.
Handle old prints with clean, dry hands, and use copies for fragile or valuable photos.
Keep the album on a steady surface so it cannot slide off a lap or tray.
Check photos for addresses or other private details before showing them to visitors or sharing them online.
activities.stopNote: It is fine to stop after one page. Close the album, leave it on the table, and talk about something else or sit quietly together.

variations.text: Choose four to six pictures beforehand, one to a page, with a large word written on a sticky note. The person picks which page to look at.
Use a small album on a lap tray and turn the pages for them, keeping each session to a few pictures.
Use enlarged copies in bold, high-contrast prints, and read any captions aloud.
A grandchild turns the pages and asks the older adult about each picture, then writes down the stories they choose to share.
Use a book stand or a folded towel to hold the album open, and turn each page with a sweep of the flat hand instead of a pinch.

activities.title: Make a beaded keyring
activities.summary: Thread a few large beads onto a cord, tie it off and fasten it to a keyring to carry or give.
steps: Before you start, the helper cuts the cord to about 12 inches, and wraps one end in clear tape.
Tie a loose knot in the other end of the cord so the beads stay on.
Place the beads in the tray, inside the raised edges, in front of the person.
Slide one bead at a time onto the taped end, counting as you go.
Stop when the beads fill about half the cord, leaving a few inches free.
Tie a firm knot at the free end, so the beads cannot slide off.
Loop the knotted end through the split keyring, and tie a knot to hold it.
Put the beads back in the tray, and count them out and back in.
plainSteps: Before you start, the helper cuts the cord to about 12 inches.

Tie a knot to hold it.

Strong string or cord, about 12 inches long
A split keyring
Clear tape to stiffen one end of the cord
Scissors for the helper only
A tray with raised edges
safety: Beads and small pieces are a choking hazard for children under three and for anyone who mouths things. Do not use beads with an under-three or with anyone who mouths objects.
Use large beads only after the person's safety has been considered. Keep loose beads in the tray, and count them out and back in.
Keep the cord short, and do not hang the keyring round a neck or leave it where an under-three can reach it.
Do not use resin or epoxy to hold or seal beads. The fumes and skin contact are a hazard.
Scissors are for the helper only.
An adult stays nearby, and checks every knot before the keyring is used so that no bead can come loose.
activities.stopNote: It is fine to stop with a few beads on the cord. Tie a knot, put the beads back in the tray and count them, and finish another day, or leave it as it is.

variations.text: The helper ties the knots and tapes the end, so the person only slides the beads on and says when to stop.
Sit at a table with the tray in front of you, and rest your elbows on the table while you thread.
Use a dark cord with pale beads, or the reverse, so each bead stands out clearly against the cord.
Use beads with the biggest holes you can find, and let the helper tie the knots so the fingers do not have to pinch.
Each person makes one keyring from the same tray, and the group compares them at the end.

activities.title: Make a button picture
activities.summary: Sort buttons by color or size and glue them onto card to make a simple picture.
steps: Count the buttons onto the tray before you start and note the number.
Draw a simple outline on the card together, or choose a shape you like.
Look through the buttons together and sort a few by color or size if they enjoy it.
Ask where the first button should go. Any place is the right one.
Add a dot of glue and press the button down together.
Keep adding buttons, taking turns choosing and placing.
Leave the picture flat to dry somewhere safe.
Count the loose buttons back into their container and check the number matches.

A pencil for a simple outline, such as a tree or a flower
A shallow tray or plate to hold the buttons
safety: Buttons are a choking hazard. Skip this activity if the person may put small objects in their mouth; use paper circles instead.
Use large buttons only, keep the number small, and count them in and out so none go missing.
To reduce the risk further, glue the buttons onto the card yourself first and use the activity for arranging and talking.
Stay at the table the whole time; do not leave loose buttons within reach of the person or young children.
Use a glue stick or white craft glue rather than hot glue, and check for skin sensitivity first.
activities.stopNote: It is fine to stop after one or two buttons. Count the loose ones away, leave the picture to dry, and offer to add more another day.

variations.text: Glue only three to five buttons, or glue them for them and let the person choose each spot.
Use bright buttons on dark card, or dark buttons on white card, so each one stands out clearly.
Offer only a few buttons in one or two colors on a plain tray, so there is less to look at and choose from.
A child applies the glue while the older adult picks the buttons and the spots. Keep buttons away from young children.
Hold up two buttons and watch which one they reach for or look at. Pointing and nodding are full answers.
Use large, flat buttons with a wide edge, and press each one down with the flat of a thumb or a small sponge instead of a pinch.

activities.title: Make a color collage
activities.summary: Choose one color, tear out magazine pieces in that color and glue them onto card.
steps: Clear a table, then lay out the card, the glue stick and a pile of magazines.
Choose one color together, such as blue, yellow or green. Any choice is fine.
Turn the pages and find pictures or patches in that color, then tear out the ones you like.
Tear each piece into a rough shape, since torn edges look softer than cut ones.
Glue the back of one piece and press it onto the card.
Keep adding pieces and let them overlap, so the color builds up.
Stop when the card feels full, then press it flat under a heavy book for a few minutes.

safety: Tearing is the main method, so scissors stay with the helper.
Use a glue stick, which is less messy than liquid glue, and check for skin sensitivity first.
Torn paper edges can nick fingers. Check hands at the end, and wipe glue from the fingers.
Keep small pieces of paper away from the mouth.
activities.stopNote: It is fine to stop after a handful of pieces. Leave the card on the table where it is easy to see, and carry on another time or simply enjoy the color.

variations.text: Offer a choice between two colors, and tear the first few pieces together.
Work on a clipboard or lap tray with a small stack of pieces already torn.
Choose a strong, bright color and work on a dark or white card so each piece stands out clearly.
Hold up two colors and watch where the eyes or hand go. Pointing and nodding are full answers.
A child tears and glues the pieces while the older adult chooses where each one goes.
Use a large glue stick, or wrap a regular one in tape to make it thicker. Tear wide pieces so each one can be lifted in the palm.

activities.title: Make a family tree of hands
activities.summary: Trace family members' hands in pencil around a drawn trunk to make a shared tree.
steps: Tape the paper to the table and draw a simple tree trunk and branches together.
Ask who would like to go first. Anyone may choose not to be traced.
Rest one person's hand flat on the paper near a branch, fingers spread comfortably.
Trace around the hand gently with a pencil.
Write that person's name inside or beside the hand.
Repeat for each person who wants to join, taking turns.
Color in the hands together, one color or many, as you like.
Hang or keep the tree somewhere everyone can see it.

Write that person's name inside or beside the hand.

Hang the tree or keep it somewhere everyone can see.
materials: A large sheet of paper or poster board
A pencil for tracing
Colored pencils, crayons or markers for coloring in
A brown marker or crayon for the trunk
Masking tape to hold the paper still
safety: Trace with a pencil only and never put paint or ink on skin. Some skin bruises or tears easily, so trace gently and lift away from the hand.
Ask before touching anyone's hand. If spreading fingers is painful, trace the hand relaxed or as a mitten shape.
Family trees can bring up people who have died, separation or estrangement. Include anyone they want and let them lead.
Keep markers away from skin; washable markers come off with soap and water.
activities.stopNote: It is fine to stop after one hand. Add more names whenever family visits, or keep the tree as it is. Every version is complete.

variations.text: Trace just two hands, for example a grandparent and a grandchild, side by side on a smaller sheet.
Children trace the older adult's hand and the older adult traces theirs. Add the children's ages or a word each.
In a group, each person traces their own hand on a separate sheet and adds it to a large shared tree on the wall.
Bring the paper to the person on a lap tray or clipboard, so they need not move to the table.
Go over each pencil outline with a thick dark marker afterward so the shapes are easy to see.
Trace with a thick crayon or a pencil wrapped in tape, and color in with jumbo crayons held in the whole hand.

activities.title: Make a festival decoration
activities.summary: Make a paper lantern, star, garland or card for a celebration the two of you choose, in your own way.
steps: Ask which celebration or season they would like to make something for. It can be from their own tradition, a different one, or simply a time of year they enjoy.
Offer a few ideas, such as a lantern, a star, a garland, a card for a new year, or a harvest or spring decoration, and let them choose or suggest their own.
Check before starting. If a symbol or object is sacred to them, ask whether they want it made as a craft, and choose something else if not.
Lay out paper in colors that suit the celebration and let them pick the ones they like.
The helper cuts the paper to size. Fold, roll or loop it together into the chosen shape.
Glue or tape the pieces where needed. They press and hold while you secure it.
Decorate with pens or crayons, adding patterns, symbols or words they choose.
Choose where to hang or stand it, and hang it together with string or ribbon.

Glue or tape the pieces where needed.
They press and hold while you secure it.
Decorate with pens or crayons.
Add patterns, symbols or words they choose.
Choose where to hang or stand it.
Hang it together with string or ribbon.

Scissors for the helper
A glue stick or removable tape
Pens, crayons or markers for decorating
String or ribbon for hanging
safety: Keep scissors with the helper, and put them away between steps.
Do not use candles or real flames, in or near the decoration. Hang paper away from heaters, lamps and stoves.
Check for sensitivity to glue, tape or marker fumes. Use a glue stick and keep the room ventilated.
Hang it where it will not catch on a walker, wheelchair or feet. Use a steady step stool, never a chair.
activities.stopNote: It is fine to stop at any point. A half-made lantern or a single star is still lovely, and you can come back to it, or put it away, whenever they wish.

variations.text: Make just one piece: a single paper star, a folded card or one lantern. The helper prepares the cut paper and they choose the colors and decorate.
Work on a lap tray or a table at a comfortable height. Keep paper, tape and pens within easy reach, and rest whenever needed.
Use thick markers or crayons and large pieces of paper. Press folds flat with the palm and close seams with wide tape instead of pinching.
Each person makes one piece for a celebration of their own choosing, then hang them together as a shared display of different traditions.
Use bold, high-contrast paper, such as dark on pale, with thick markers. Describe each piece aloud as you hand it over.

activities.title: Make a friendship bracelet
activities.summary: Braid three thick strands of yarn into a simple bracelet or bookmark tassel, taped to the table.
steps: Lay the three strands side by side and tie one loose knot at the top, leaving a tail of about two inches.
Tape the knot to the table or tray so it stays still.
Spread the three strands apart, with one on each side and one in the middle.
Take the right strand and lay it over the middle one.
Take the left strand and lay it over the new middle one.
Keep going, right over middle, then left over middle, pulling each strand snug but not tight.
When the braid is long enough to go around the wrist or lie in a book, tie a loose knot at the end.
Trim the ends to a short tassel, or tie the bracelet around a wrist loosely. The helper does the trimming.

Scissors for the helper only
Masking tape to hold the strands to the table
A clipboard or a tray for a lap
safety: Scissors are for the helper only. Cut the strands before you start and put the scissors away.
Keep strands short, never wrap yarn around a neck, and take a bracelet off if it feels tight. Keep long strands away from the neck.
Loose ends can be swallowed or chewed. Supervise if anyone might put yarn or tassel ends in the mouth.
Choose soft yarn that does not itch or irritate sensitive skin, and gather up loose yarn so nobody trips on it.
activities.stopNote: It is fine to stop whenever you like. Tape the end down, leave the braid on the table, and pick it up another day, or leave it as a short bookmark.

variations.text: Start the braid ahead of time and use only two or three crossings together, or braid with one color on a chunky cord.
Use very thick yarn or strips of cotton fabric, and braid with the whole hand. Make a long bookmark instead of a wrist-sized bracelet.
Tape the knot to a clipboard on a lap tray and braid for a few minutes at a time, putting the yarn down whenever you like.
Use three strongly different colors on a plain dark surface, and say each move aloud: right over, left over.
A child holds the knot steady while the grandparent braids, then swap. Choose the three colors together.

activities.title: Make a greeting card
activities.summary: A folded card with a picture on the front and a short message inside, made for someone you both know.
steps: Talk together about who the card is for, such as a grandchild, a neighbor or an old friend.
Lay out four or five pictures and ask which one suits that person.
Glue the chosen picture to the front of the folded card.
Open the card and ask what they would like to say. A few words are plenty.
Write the message, or let them write it if they prefer.
Ask whether they would like to sign it, add a mark, or have you sign for both of you.
Put the card in the envelope and agree together when to send or deliver it.
plainSteps: Talk about who the card is for.

Pictures cut from old cards, magazines or seed packets
A glue stick
A thick felt-tip pen or marker
An envelope
safety: If you cut pictures, keep the scissors with the helper.
A glue stick is less messy than liquid glue; check for skin sensitivity first.
Do not ask anyone to write if it is tiring or upsetting. Dictating the message counts fully.
activities.stopNote: It is fine to stop with just a picture on the front. Keep the card in a safe place and finish the message another day, or send it as it is.

variations.text: Glue the picture on before you start, so the only choice is what to say or who to send it to.
Use bright card, one large picture, and a thick black marker so letters stand out clearly.
A child writes out the message while the older adult decides the words and chooses the picture.
Make one large card together for a shared friend or staff member, with each person adding a picture or a word.
Offer two finished messages written on slips of paper and let them point to the one they like.
Wrap the pen in a foam hair curler or a few layers of tape, or use a thick felt-tip marker. The helper can write the words if the hand tires.

activities.title: Make a lavender sachet
activities.summary: Spoon dried lavender onto a square of fabric and tie it into a small scented bundle.
steps: Set the tray on the table and pour the lavender into the bowl.
Offer the bowl to smell, and ask if they would like to make a sachet with it.
Lay the fabric square flat on the tray, patterned side down.
Spoon lavender into the middle of the fabric together.
Gather the four corners up into a small bundle.
Hold the bundle while one person wraps the ribbon around the neck.
Tie the ribbon in a knot or a bow. The helper can do this.
Decide together where the sachet should go, such as a drawer or a coat pocket.

Two or three spoonfuls of dried lavender

A small bowl and a teaspoon

Do not put the sachet near a heater, radiator or open flame.
activities.stopNote: It is fine to stop at any point. A bowl of lavender to smell is enough on its own. Cover the bowl and offer to finish the sachet another day.

variations.text: Fill the bundle beforehand and leave only the ribbon to tie, or offer a choice between two fabrics and two ribbons.
Use a lap tray with raised edges and a pre-filled spoon. Make one small sachet and tie it loosely together.
Skip the lavender and fill the sachet with plain dried rice or beans, so it is something to hold with no scent.
Use a bright fabric on a dark tray, and a thick, textured ribbon that is easy to find and grip.
A child spoons and gathers the fabric while the older adult chooses the fabric and ties or holds the ribbon.
The helper ties the ribbon. The person holds the bundle in an open hand, so the fabric does not need to be pinched.

activities.title: Make a memory collage
activities.summary: A relaxed creative activity using photos, magazine pictures and paper.

Look through the pictures together and talk about any that catch an eye.
Ask which picture should go in the middle. Any answer is the right one.
Glue the back of that picture and press it down together.
Add more pictures around it, taking turns choosing and placing.
Stop when it feels finished, or when you have had enough for today.
Agree on a place to keep or show the collage, such as a fridge or a frame.

activities.title: Make a paper chain garland
activities.summary: A long garland of looped paper strips, made one link at a time and hung up to brighten a room.
steps: Cut paper into strips about one inch wide and eight inches long before you begin.
Lay the strips out and ask which colors or patterns to use.
Bend one strip into a loop and glue or tape the ends together.
Thread the next strip through the first loop.
Close the second loop, so the two links are joined.
Keep adding links, taking turns or with one person threading and the other closing.
Hold the chain up together now and then to see how long it has grown.
Decide together where to hang it, such as a window, a doorway or across a mantel.

A ruler and pencil
Removable tape or hooks for hanging
safety: Keep scissors, staplers and paper trimmers with the helper.
Hang the finished garland well away from candles, heaters and lamps.
Hang it high enough that it will not catch on walkers, wheelchairs or feet, and use a steady step stool, not a chair.
activities.stopNote: It is fine to stop after a few links. A short chain still looks cheerful on a doorknob, and you can add to it any time; it never needs to be finished.

variations.text: The helper threads each strip through, and the participant presses the ends together to close the loop.
Each person makes a short chain in their own colors, then everyone joins the chains into one long garland.
Write a name, a word or a favorite thing on each strip before making the loop.
Use wider strips in two strongly contrasting colors and alternate them to make the pattern easy to follow.
Work on a lap tray and let the finished chain fall into a box at your feet as it grows.
Use wider strips and a roll of wide tape to close each loop, so the ends are pressed together with the palm instead of pinched.

activities.title: Make a personal songbook
activities.summary: Collect favorite songs, a few lines of words and the stories behind them in one book.
steps: Sit together and open the book to a blank page.
Ask about a song they enjoy, or offer a choice of two familiar songs.
Play the song at a comfortable volume and listen together.
Write the song title at the top of the page.
Add the singer or a favorite line, if they want to.
Invite a story about the song, such as where they heard it or who they danced with.
Write a few words about the story, in their words.
Play the song again if they would like, or choose the next one.

activities.title: Make a photo postcard
activities.summary: Glue a copy of a favorite photo onto card, then write one line together.
steps: Look through the photo copies together and choose one to send.
Place the photo on the card to see how it fits, and ask the helper to trim it if needed.
Glue the back of the photo and press it onto the card.
Press the photo flat with a hand and hold it for a few seconds.
Ask who the card is for, and what one line they would like to write.
Write the line on the back of the card, in the words the person chooses, and sign it together.
If sending, put the card in an envelope with the address and a stamp.
plainSteps: Look through the photo copies together.

A postcard-sized piece of thick card, or a blank postcard
A glue stick
A pen with a thick grip

safety: Use photo copies only, so an original is never cut, glued or lost.
Use a glue stick, which is less messy than liquid glue, and check for skin sensitivity first.
Check the address before sealing the envelope. Never write bank details or passwords on a card.
activities.stopNote: It is fine to stop after choosing the photo. Keep the copy somewhere handy and carry on another day, or simply look at it together.

variations.text: Choose the photo and have the card already trimmed, and offer one or two suggested lines to pick from.
Work on a clipboard or lap tray, with a card already cut to size.
Choose a photo with strong contrast and large details, and write the line in a thick dark marker.
A child picks the photo and writes the name, while the older adult says the line to write.
Wrap a thin pen in a few layers of tape, or use a thick marker. Press the photo flat with the whole palm instead of the fingertips.

activities.title: Make a pine cone bird feeder
activities.summary: Spread fat on a pine cone, roll it in birdseed and hang it outside to watch the birds.
steps: Cover the table and set out the pine cone, the fat and the dish of seed.
Tie the string around the top of the pine cone. The helper can do this.
Spread fat into the gaps of the cone with the spoon or knife.
Roll the cone in the dish of seed together, pressing it in.
Sprinkle any bare patches with more seed by hand.
Choose a branch or hook that can be seen from a window or chair.
Hang the feeder there together, or let them watch while you hang it.
Sit by the window and see which birds arrive, if you like.
plainSteps: Cover the table.
Set out the pine cone, the fat and the dish of seed.

Vegetable shortening, or peanut butter if nobody has a nut allergy
Wild birdseed in a shallow dish

String or garden twine, about 18 inches
Newspaper or a tray to work on
Wet wipes or a damp cloth
safety: Peanut butter can cause a severe allergic reaction. Ask about nut allergies first, and use vegetable shortening if anyone is unsure.
Birdseed is not food for people, and small seeds can be a choking risk. Supervise if anything might be put in the mouth.
Keep any knife blunt, or use a spoon. Wash hands after handling seed and fat.
Hang the feeder from the ground or a stable step, never a chair or ladder. Keep paths clear outdoors to prevent falls.
Pine cones collected outdoors can have sharp scales and sap. Choose dry, open ones and check them first.
activities.stopNote: It is fine to stop once the cone has a little seed on it. The birds will not mind. Hang it as it is, or leave it on a tray and finish another day.

variations.text: The helper spreads the fat first. The only job is rolling the cone in seed, or sprinkling seed on with fingers.
Make the whole feeder at the table, then hang it outside a window that can be seen from a favorite chair.
Wear thin gloves or use a spoon to press seed on, so hands stay clean and the fat is never touched.
A child does the rolling and sprinkling while the older adult chooses the spot and names the birds that visit.
Make one feeder each and hang them all on the same tree, then watch together from indoors.
Spread the fat with a wide spoon that has a thick handle, and press the seed on with the palm instead of the fingers.

activities.title: Make a playlist together
activities.summary: Choose a few favorite songs together on a phone, play each one and write the ones they like on a card.
steps: Sit together with the phone, the card and the pen in reach.
Ask what kind of music they enjoy, or offer two familiar styles to choose from.
Find one song they name, or pick one from the choices you offered.
Play the song at a comfortable volume and listen together.
Ask whether they like it.
Write the title on the card if they say yes.
Choose the next song together, and repeat until the card has five to eight titles.
Read the list aloud and ask which song they would like to hear first.

A small card, index card or sheet of paper
A thick pen or marker

Turn off autoplay video and ads before you start, so the music does not change to something unexpected.
activities.stopNote: It is fine to stop after one or two songs. Leave the card as it is, play something gentle, or simply sit and listen together for a while.

variations.text: Choose three or four songs in advance and offer them as simple yes or no choices. The helper handles the phone and writes the titles.
Prop the phone on a stand or pillow at a low volume, and keep the card on a clipboard. The helper handles the screen.
Write the titles in large, high-contrast letters, or read them aloud from the screen. Choose songs by sound rather than by picture.
A grandchild finds the songs and plays them, while the older adult says what they like and the child writes the titles on the card.
Prop the phone or tablet in a stand so it does not need holding, and write the titles with a thick marker or a pen wrapped in tape.

activities.title: Make a sealed shaker
activities.summary: Fill a small sealed bottle with dried rice, decorate it and shake along to a favorite song.
steps: Sit at a table with the bottle, rice, funnel and decorations in reach.
Pour in a small handful of rice, enough to fill about a quarter of the bottle.
Ask the helper to glue the lid shut, then wrap tape firmly over it.
Decorate the outside with tape, paper or stickers, one piece at a time, while the glue dries.
Leave the shaker to dry fully, overnight if possible, and check the lid is firm.
Next time, play a song and hold the shaker so it is easy to move.
Shake gently in time with the beat, then try a slower shake.
Set the shaker down and store it out of reach of anyone who puts things in their mouth.

A small handful of dried rice
A funnel, or a folded piece of paper to guide the rice
Craft glue and strong tape for sealing the lid
Colored tape, paper or stickers for decoration
A phone or player with a steady song
safety: Glue the lid shut and tape over it, then check the lid before each use. Replace the shaker if the lid loosens or the bottle cracks.
Never make or use this with someone who puts things in their mouth. Keep the shaker away from anyone who may chew or swallow small grains.
Fill with dried rice only. Do not add small beads, coins, buttons or other small items, which can be swallowed.
Sweep up spilled rice at once, because loose grains on the floor are a slip hazard.
Stay close while the shaker is used, and keep it out of reach of anyone who may put it in their mouth.
Check for food allergies before using rice or any grain, and wash hands after handling it.
activities.stopNote: It is fine to stop after the first shake, or before the decoration is finished. Put the shaker on the shelf and finish it another day.

variations.text: The helper fills, seals and decorates the bottle beforehand. The only job is to shake it along to a song and say which tempo they like.
Put in only a few grains, so the sound is soft. Hold the sealed shaker on the lap and feel its weight and gentle movement.
A child chooses the decorations and presses the tape down, while the older adult fills the bottle with rice and picks the song.
Choose a bottle with a wide, ridged cap, and let the helper screw and tape the lid. Hold the bottle in both hands while you shake it.

activities.title: Make a texture board
activities.summary: Glue different textures onto a sturdy board to make something interesting to touch and look at.
steps: Lay the textured scraps out on the table in a row.
Pass each one over and feel it together, saying what it is like if you wish.
Ask which texture they would like to put on the board first.
Spread glue on the back of that piece. The helper can do this.
Press it onto the board together and hold for a few seconds.
Add more pieces, taking turns choosing where each one goes.
Leave the board flat to dry, as the glue bottle suggests.
Run your hands across the finished board together and talk about favorites.
plainSteps: Lay the textured scraps out in a row.
Pass each one over and feel it together.
Say what it is like, if you wish.
Ask which texture they would like on the board first.
Spread glue on the back of that piece.
The helper can do this.
Press it onto the board together.
Hold it for a few seconds.
Add more pieces.
Take turns choosing where each one goes.
Leave the board flat to dry, as the glue bottle suggests.
Run your hands across the finished board together.
Talk about favorites.
materials: A piece of sturdy cardboard, about letter size
Six to ten textured scraps: corduroy, felt, velvet, burlap, ribbon, sponge
A few household textures, such as a bottle cap, a button or a strip of bubble wrap
White craft glue or a hot glue gun for the helper
Scissors for the helper
safety: Glue all pieces firmly. Buttons, caps and beads are choking risks if they come loose and might be put in the mouth.
If small pieces might be mouthed, leave out buttons and caps and use only large fabric pieces.
Keep any hot glue gun and scissors with the helper. Let hot glue cool fully before the board is handled.
Avoid sharp edges such as cut plastic, wire or sandpaper; check the board by hand before handing it over.
activities.stopNote: It is fine to stop after one or two pieces. Feeling the scraps together is the activity too. Set the board aside to finish later, or keep it as it is.

variations.text: Cut all the pieces to the same size beforehand and offer two at a time. Choosing is the main job.
Glue the pieces in advance and bring the finished board to the bedside. Explore it together by touch, one square at a time.
Use strongly contrasting colors and very different textures, such as smooth satin next to rough burlap.
Use only soft, quiet fabrics and leave out anything crinkly, scratchy or noisy like bubble wrap.
Each person adds one texture to a shared board, then you pass it around and compare favorites.
A child finds and sorts the textures; the grandparent decides where each one goes. Use white glue only, and keep any hot glue gun with an adult.

activities.title: Make a tissue paper window picture
activities.summary: Press torn pieces of colored tissue paper onto clear sticky film, then hang it in a window to let light shine through.
steps: Before you start, the helper cuts the film to size, peels off the backing and tapes it sticky side up to the table.
Put the bowls of tissue pieces within easy reach.
Choose a color together. Any color is a good one.
Pick up a piece and press it onto the sticky film anywhere you like.
Add more pieces, and let them overlap so the colors mix.
Stop when the picture feels full or you are ready to be done.
The helper lays a second piece of film over the top or folds the first one in half, and smooths it down.
Hang the picture in a window and look at the light coming through.
plainSteps: Before you start, the helper cuts the film to size.
The helper peels off the backing.
The helper tapes it sticky side up to the table.
Put the bowls of tissue pieces within easy reach.
Choose a color together.
Any color is a good one.
Pick up a piece.
Press it onto the sticky film anywhere you like.
Add more pieces so the colors overlap and mix.
Stop when it feels full or you are ready to be done.
The helper lays a second piece of film over the top.
Or the helper folds the first one in half.
The helper smooths it down.
Hang it in a window.
Look at the light coming through.
materials: Clear self-adhesive film (contact film), cut by the helper to about letter size
Colored tissue paper, torn beforehand into pieces about the size of a palm
Two or three shallow bowls to sort the colors
Masking tape, for the helper to hold the film and to hang it
Scissors, for the helper to use beforehand only
safety: The helper cuts the film with scissors beforehand and puts them away. The person does not cut anything.
Keep small torn tissue pieces and the film away from the mouth, and stay nearby while they are out. Clear them away afterward.
Check for sensitivity to the sticky film or tape, and keep the sticky side off bare skin and hair.
The helper hangs the picture, using a stable chair or step stool if needed. The person does not climb or lean out.
activities.stopNote: It is fine to stop with only a few pieces on the film. A sparse picture lets in plenty of light, and you can add more another day.

variations.text: Offer one color at a time in a single bowl, and place the first piece together.
Tape the film to a lap tray or a tray table at a comfortable height, with the bowls on the same tray.
Use big pieces of tissue, about the size of a whole hand, so they can be held in a fist and pressed down with the flat of the palm.
Use strong, dark colors such as deep blue, red and green, and hang the picture where the sun is bright.
Tape the film sticky side up to a firm tray on the bed table, with one bowl of pieces. The helper holds the tray steady and hangs the picture by the bed.
The older adult chooses each color and where it goes, and the child hands over the pieces and presses them flat. Cutting stays with an adult.

activities.title: Make a torn paper landscape
activities.summary: Tear long strips of colored paper and layer them into sky, hills and ground.
steps: Lay the card flat in front of the person, with the long side across if they prefer.
Tear a few long strips of pale blue or white paper for the sky and place them in a tray.
Tear strips in greens for hills, and strips in browns or yellows for the ground.
Rub glue on the top third of the card and press the sky strips on, letting them overlap.
Glue the middle of the card and press on the green strips, tearing a wavy edge along the top for hills.
Glue the bottom and add the ground strips, overlapping the bottom of the hills.
Add a torn round of yellow paper for a sun, or a few small green scraps for trees, if wanted.
Press the picture flat with a clean hand and leave it to dry, then choose where to put it.

Work on a lap tray with a raised edge so the strips do not slide off, with the card held in place by a non-slip mat.
Use a small piece of card on a lap tray, with a few strips already torn and a glue stick within easy reach.
Use a thick glue stick, or wrap a regular one in foam so it is easy to hold. Tear wide strips that can be picked up in the whole hand.
Choose strongly contrasting colors, such as dark blue sky above bright green hills, and say each color aloud as it is placed.
A child tears the strips and hands them over while the older adult decides which strip goes where and glues it down.

activities.title: Make leaf rubbings
activities.summary: Lay leaves under thin paper and rub with the side of a crayon until the veins appear.
steps: Set out the leaves, paper and crayons on a tray or at the table.
Choose a leaf together and look at it. Any leaf is a good leaf.
Lay the leaf vein-side up on the tray.
Cover the leaf with a sheet of paper and tape the paper corners to the tray so it stays still.
Peel the wrapper off a crayon and hold it flat, on its side.
Rub gently over the leaf in one direction until the veins and edge come up.
Lift the paper to look. Try a second leaf, or the same leaf in another color.
Lay the finished rubbings side by side to look at together.
plainSteps: Set out the leaves, paper and crayons.
Choose a leaf together.

Lay the leaf vein-side up on the tray.
Cover the leaf with a sheet of paper.

Peel the wrapper off a crayon.
Hold the crayon flat, on its side.

Lift the paper to look.
Try a second leaf, or the same leaf in another color.

Look at them together.

Thin paper, such as copy paper or tracing paper
Wax crayons with the paper wrapper peeled off, used on their sides
A tray or a clipboard
Low-tack masking tape to hold the paper still
safety: Use leaves from a garden, a park or a houseplant that you know. Do not pick wild plants that could be poisonous, and avoid poison ivy, poison oak and sumac.
Check for plant allergies and skin sensitivity before handling leaves, and wash hands afterward.
Keep leaves and crayons away from the mouth. Do not let anyone chew or taste them.
Use low-tack tape on the paper only, and take it off gently so the paper does not tear.

activities.title: Match colors to a tune
activities.summary: Listen to a short tune together, then pick the colors that seem to go with it and lay them in a row.

Ask which tune they would like first, or offer two to choose from.
Play the tune at a comfortable volume and listen together.
When it ends, ask which color seems to go with it, and let them pick one or a few.
Lay the chosen colors in a row on the tray. Any color is a good answer.
Play the next tune and start a new row beside the first.
Look at the rows together, and keep the one they like best if they wish.
plainSteps: Spread the colored squares where they can see them all.
Ask which tune they would like first.
Or offer two to choose from.
Play the tune at a comfortable volume.
Listen together.
When it ends, ask which color seems to go with it.
Let them pick one or a few.

Start a new row beside the first.
Look at the rows together.

Three or four short tunes they like, in different styles

A tray or a sheet of plain paper to lay the colors on

Turn off autoplay and ads so the music does not change without warning.

activities.title: Move to music in a chair
activities.summary: Move gently in a chair to a tune they choose: tap feet, sway, roll shoulders or wave a scarf to the beat.
steps: Set a sturdy chair with no wheels on a flat, clear floor, with nothing to trip over around it.
Ask what tune they would like. Offer two or three choices, or let them pick their own.
Help them sit back with both feet flat on the floor, and play the tune at a comfortable volume.
Start with something small, such as tapping one foot or a hand on the knee, and let them copy or lead.
Try one movement at a time: sway side to side, roll the shoulders, or reach a scarf up and down.
Move at their pace and in their way. There is no right shape and nothing to count.
Move along with them, and follow any movement they come up with.
Let the song end, then sit quietly together and offer a drink of water.
plainSteps: Set a sturdy chair with no wheels on a flat floor.
Clear anything they could trip over around the chair.
Ask what tune they would like.
Offer two or three choices, or let them pick.
Help them sit back with both feet flat on the floor.
Play the tune at a comfortable volume.
Start small, such as tapping one foot.
Let them copy you or lead.
Try one movement at a time.
Sway side to side, roll the shoulders or reach a scarf up.
Move at their pace and in their way.
Follow any movement they come up with.
Let the song end.
Sit quietly together.
Offer a drink of water.
materials: A tune they choose, saved on a phone or player, or a song you can sing together
A sturdy chair without wheels, with arms if they prefer
A light scarf or a strip of soft cloth, if they like
Clear floor space around the chair
safety: Keep them seated in a stable chair with no wheels, feet flat on the floor. Do not ask them to stand up and dance.
Pain means stop. Never ask for more movement than they offer, and do not count repetitions.
This is not exercise or rehabilitation. Check with their doctor or care team before any new movement.
Stay within arm's reach and keep the space around the chair clear. Keep the scarf away from the neck.
Pause if they look tired, short of breath or unsteady, and offer a drink of water.
activities.stopNote: It is fine to stop after one song, or after a few bars. Turn the music down, sit quietly together and say that was lovely, or simply that is enough for now.

variations.text: Only tap a foot or a hand to the beat, or simply listen while you move. Joining in for a few moments is enough.
Lying or propped up, move only the hands and arms: wave a scarf, tap the blanket or sway the fingers to the tune. No need to sit upright.
Use no talking. Show a movement, wait, and copy whatever they do back to them. A smile or a tapped foot says yes.
Pick a slow, quiet tune and turn the volume low. Keep the room still and move one hand at a time.
Use a bright scarf against a plain background. Say what you are doing in a few words and rest a hand lightly on theirs to share the beat.
Choose a chair with arms and sit beside them, not in front, so they can follow your movement from the side.

activities.title: Paint a garden stone
activities.summary: A smooth stone painted with simple colors or patterns, then placed outdoors where you both can see it.
steps: Wash the stones and let them dry before you start.
Set out two or three stones and ask which one they would like to paint.
Pick one or two colors together.
Paint a base color over the top of the stone, or leave the natural stone showing.
Add a simple pattern if you both like, such as dots, stripes, a flower or a single initial.
Leave the stone to dry for about an hour, then add a second coat if you want stronger color.
Choose a spot together where the stone will sit, such as a flower bed, a doorstep or a window ledge.
Carry the stone out and place it, or have it carried out if walking is tiring.

Children gather and wash the stones, and everyone paints one to set out together in a row.
Each person paints a stone and the group arranges them along a path or around a planter.
Use a sponge or a thick foam brush in place of a small brush, and hold it in the whole hand to dab on dots or stripes.

activities.title: Paint a shared picture
activities.summary: Paint one large picture together, with everyone adding a mark in turn.
steps: Cover the table with a plastic cloth, then tape the large paper flat over it at all four corners.
Set out the paints, brushes and water cups so everyone can reach them.
Ask each person what they would like to begin with, such as a sky, a shape, a line or a color. Any choice is fine.
Let everyone make a first mark anywhere on the paper.
Take turns adding one mark or shape at a time, and pause to look at the whole picture between turns.
Rinse the brush in the water cup before changing color.
Stop when the picture feels finished, then leave it flat to dry.
When the paint is dry, remove the tape and choose a place to hang the picture.

Non-toxic, water-based paint or washable poster paint in several colors
Brushes, sponges and a few cotton swabs
A cup of water for each person
A plastic tablecloth or old towels under the paper
Masking tape and paper towels
safety: Use non-toxic, water-based paint only, and check for any known paint allergies first.
Keep brushes and small items away from the mouth, and do not let anyone drink from the water cups.
Put towels or a plastic cloth under the paper, and wipe up spills at once so no one slips.
Wash hands after painting, and keep paint away from the face if skin is sensitive.
Stay close while paint and brushes are in use, and keep the water cups out of reach of anyone who may drink from them.
activities.stopNote: It is fine to stop after one mark. Leave the picture where it is, and carry on another time, or simply enjoy the marks made so far.

variations.text: Give each person one color and a sponge, so they only need to dab the paper.
Work on a clipboard or tilted board on the lap, with a large sponge and one or two colors.
Use bold, high-contrast colors on white paper, and describe each mark out loud as it goes on.
Divide a large sheet into sections, one for each person, and join the sections into one picture at the end.
Give the child and the grandparent a corner each to start, then let the marks meet in the middle. Wash brushes together at the end.
Give each person a large sponge or a foam roller in place of a brush, held in the whole hand.

activities.title: Paint with watercolors
activities.summary: Loose, colorful washes of watercolor paint on paper, where blending and running colors are the whole point.
steps: Cover the table with the towel or newspaper and set out the paint, brushes and water.
Ask which two or three colors they would like to use today.
Brush clean water over the whole sheet of paper together.
Dip a brush in one color and touch it to the wet paper.
Watch together as the color spreads, then add a second color next to it.
Tilt the paper gently if you both want the colors to run and mix.
Talk about what the shapes look like, such as a sky, a field or nothing at all.
Leave the painting flat to dry and decide together whether to paint another.
