safety: Use only non-toxic, water-based paint, and keep the painting water separate from any drinking cups.
Some people put brushes in their mouth; stay close and use clearly different cups for paint water and drinks.
Wash paint off skin with warm water and soap, and check first for any skin sensitivity.
Wipe up spilled water promptly so floors do not become slippery.
activities.stopNote: It is fine to stop after one wash of color. Leave the paper to dry somewhere flat and offer to paint again another day, or simply look at it together.

variations.text: Wet the paper and load the brush in advance, so the only task is touching the brush to the page.
Tape the paper to a clipboard, use a lidded water pot, and keep to one color at a time.
Choose strong, dark colors such as deep blue and red on bright white paper, and use a desk lamp.
Paint a sheet each, side by side, then swap and add a color to each other's painting.
Hold up two paint colors and wait for a look, a reach or a nod. That choice is the whole conversation.
Wrap each brush handle with tape or foam to make it thicker, so it can be held in a full fist.

activities.title: Plant seeds in a pot
activities.summary: Fill a pot with soil, press in a few large seeds and water them together.
steps: Spread newspaper or a tray on the table and set the pot on it.
Spoon potting mix into the pot together until it is nearly full.
Press the soil down gently with flat hands.
Show the seeds and ask which ones they would like to plant.
Push each seed into the soil about as deep as a fingertip.
Cover the seeds with a little soil and pat it down.
Water slowly together until the soil looks dark and damp.
Choose a bright windowsill for the pot and agree who will check on it.

Bagged potting mix
A few large seeds, such as beans, peas, nasturtiums or sunflowers

A small watering can or a cup of water
Gardening gloves, if wanted

safety: Wear gloves or wash hands after handling potting mix; it can contain bacteria and fungi, and some mixes include fertilizer.
Seeds can be a choking risk and many are treated with chemicals. Supervise closely if anything might be put in the mouth.
Some seeds, such as sweet peas, are toxic if eaten. Read the packet and choose edible-garden seeds if unsure.
Outdoors, sit in the shade, offer water to drink, and keep the path clear of hoses and tools to prevent falls.
Check for allergies to seeds or plants before handling them, and wash hands afterward.
activities.stopNote: It is fine to stop after one seed. Water what is planted, put the pot somewhere bright, and finish another day if you both want to.

variations.text: Fill the pot with soil and make the holes before you start, so the only step is dropping a seed into each hole.
Work in a deep tray on a lap or table so soil stays contained and nobody needs to bend or stand.
A child fills the pot and waters while the older adult chooses the seeds and decides where the pot will live.
Wear gloves and use a spoon for everything, so hands stay clean and dry.
Use big seeds such as beans or sunflowers on a light plate, and a dark pot so the soil level is easy to see.
Use a spoon with a thick, built-up handle to make the holes, and drop large seeds such as beans in with the palm instead of a pinch.

activities.title: Press leaves and flowers
activities.summary: Gather flat leaves and flowers, then press them between paper in a heavy book together.
steps: Walk outside together or bring a few leaves and flowers to the table.
Lay them out and look at the shapes and colors together.
Ask which ones they would like to keep. Flat, dry pieces press best.
Open the book near the middle and lay a sheet of paper on the page.
Place the leaves and flowers on the paper with a little space between them.
Lay a second sheet of paper on top.
Close the book gently and stack the other books on top.
Write the date on a slip of paper and tuck it in the cover.
Agree on a day, about two weeks away, to open the book together.

materials: A handful of flat leaves and small flowers, checked as safe to handle
A large, heavy book you do not mind marking
Plain paper, paper towels or coffee filters
A few more books or a brick to add weight
A small basket or bag for collecting
safety: Some plants are toxic or irritate skin, such as foxglove, poison ivy and giant hogweed. Check every plant you pick and wash hands afterward.
Avoid holly, roses with thorns, and prickly or stinging plants.
Dried petals and seed heads are small enough to swallow. Supervise if anything might be put in the mouth.
Outdoors, choose level paths, wear sturdy shoes, and take a hat and water in the sun.
activities.stopNote: It is fine to stop after one leaf. Close the book on whatever is in it, and you will still have something to open together later.

variations.text: Collect and dry the pieces beforehand. At the table, the only choice is which leaf goes in the book next.
Bring a tray of leaves and flowers indoors and press them at the table, with no walk needed.
Each person chooses one leaf or flower for a shared book, then you open it together on a set date.
Hold up two leaves and watch where their eyes or hand go. A point or a nod is a full answer.
Choose large leaves with clear outlines, such as maple or oak, and press them on dark paper.
A child collects the leaves and places them on the paper while the grandparent picks which ones to keep. Open the book together on the agreed day.

activities.title: Print with leaves
activities.summary: Paint the back of a leaf, press it onto paper and lift it to reveal the printed veins.
steps: Cover the table with newspaper or a plastic cloth, and set out the paper, paint and brush.
Choose a leaf together and look at its veins. Any leaf is a good leaf.
Lay the leaf vein-side up on the newspaper.
Paint a thin, even layer over the veins with the brush.
Turn the leaf over and press it paint-side down onto the paper, then press gently all over with a paper towel.
Lift the leaf slowly from one edge and set it aside.
Let the print dry flat, then choose another leaf and try a different color.

Non-toxic, water-based paint or washable ink in one or two colors
A small brush or a sponge
Thick paper or card
Newspaper or a plastic cloth, and paper towels
safety: Check every leaf before handling. Avoid poison ivy, poison oak and sumac, and check for allergies.
Use non-toxic, water-based paint, and wash hands afterward.
Keep leaves and paint away from the mouth, and do not let anyone chew or taste the plants.
Pick up only fallen leaves, and never strip a living plant.
activities.stopNote: It is fine to stop after one leaf. Leave the print flat to dry and carry on later, or go for a short look at the trees nearby.

variations.text: Paint the leaf ahead of time, so the person only needs to press it onto the paper and lift it.
Work on a tray on the lap or at a low table, with the leaf held flat on a board.
Use one leaf and one color in a quiet spot, and skip handling the leaves if that feels uncomfortable.
Each person prints a leaf on one shared sheet, arranged as a wreath or a line.
A child paints the leaf and the grandparent presses it down and lifts it, then swap. Choose the colors together.
Paint the leaf with a sponge or a foam roller instead of a brush, and press it down with the flat palm.

activities.title: Print with sponge shapes
activities.summary: Press a thick sponge shape into paint, then onto paper, and lift it to see the print.
steps: Before you start, the helper cuts the sponges into big, simple shapes and puts the scissors away.
Cover the table, then set out the paper and the sponge shapes.
Pour a thin layer of paint onto each plate, one color per plate.
Choose a shape and a color together. Any choice is a good choice.
Press the sponge flat into the paint, then press it onto the paper.
Lift the sponge straight up and look at the print.
Print again in the same place or somewhere new, and change shape or color whenever you like.
Leave the paper flat to dry and choose where to show it.

Thick paper or card, plain or folded into a card
Newspaper or a plastic cloth, and paper towels

safety: The helper cuts the sponges with scissors beforehand and puts them away before the person sits down. The person does not cut anything.
Use washable, non-toxic paint, check for skin sensitivity first, and wash hands afterward.
Keep paint and sponge pieces away from the mouth, and stay nearby throughout.
Throw away any trimmings from cutting the sponges, and wipe the table and floor around the plates.
activities.stopNote: It is fine to stop after one print. Leave it to dry and put the sponges and paint away, or come back to it another day.

variations.text: Offer one shape and one color at a time, and press the first print together, hand over hand if the person wants that.
Work at a table or on a lap tray with the paper taped flat by the helper, so it stays put while the sponge is pressed.
Cut a thick sponge as wide as the palm, or push a short, thick dowel or wide wooden spoon handle into a slit in the back so it can be held in a whole fist.
Use dark paint on pale card, or bright paint on dark card, and large shapes with plain edges.
A child chooses the color and the older adult presses the shape, then swap. Keep paint plates out of reach of anyone who might taste it.

activities.title: Roll paper beads
activities.summary: Roll thin paper triangles around a pencil or straw to make colorful beads, then thread them on a string.
steps: Before you start, the helper cuts the paper into long, thin triangles, about six inches long.
Lay one triangle on the table with the wide end toward you.
Add a line of glue along the narrow end, using the glue stick.
Place the pencil or straw on the wide end, and roll the paper tightly around it.
Press the glued tip down to seal the bead, then slide it off the pencil or straw.
Let the finished beads dry for a few minutes on the table.
Make more beads, and keep them in the tray with raised edges so none roll away.
Thread each dry bead onto the string one at a time, counting each one as it goes on.
Tie a knot at each end of the string, so the beads stay on.

Use paper beads only after the person's safety has been considered. Keep the beads in the tray, and count them out and back in.
Scissors are for the helper only, and the paper is cut away from the hands.
Do not use resin or epoxy to seal or harden beads. The fumes and skin contact are a hazard.

An adult stays nearby while the beads are being made and threaded, and the finished string is never worn on the neck.
activities.stopNote: It is fine to stop after a few beads. Put them in the tray, count them, and finish another day, or leave a half-rolled bead on the table as it is.

Use a thick straw in place of a pencil, and roll with the palm of the hand rather than pinching the paper between the fingers.
Use two strongly contrasting colors of paper, and alternate them so each bead stands out against the table.
Each person rolls a set of beads in their own colors, then the group puts them together in one tray to share.

activities.title: Shape a pinch pot
activities.summary: Shape a small bowl from air-dry clay by pressing it open with your thumbs.
steps: Cover the table with a plastic cloth and put the damp cloth and the water bowl within reach.
Give each person a ball of clay about the size of a tennis ball.
Roll the clay gently between the palms until the surface is smooth.
Press a thumb into the middle to make a dip, then stop and look at it.
Turn the clay slowly and press the walls out with the thumbs, a little at a time, keeping the base flat.
Keep the walls an even thickness, about as thick as a pencil, and dampen the fingers only when the clay feels dry.
Smooth the rim with a damp finger, then wipe the fingers on the cloth.
Set the finished pot on a tray and leave it to dry for a day or two, away from direct heat.

Guide the clay with your hands over theirs, and watch for any sign they want to keep going or stop.
Choose a dark clay and work on a white tray so the shape stands out, and describe the shape aloud as you press.
Use a soft, pliable clay, and press the walls out with the side of the thumb or the whole palm instead of a pinch.

activities.title: Sketch what is on the table
activities.summary: Look at one everyday object on the table, then draw its outline with any marks you like.
steps: Place the object on the table in front of the person, where the light falls well on it.
Look at it together for a moment, and talk about its color, shape or size if they like.
Put the paper down and place the pencil in their hand, or within easy reach.
Draw the outline with a few slow lines, starting from the bottom edge. Any line is a good line.
Add a few marks inside, such as a line for a handle, a dot for a seed or a stroke for a stem.
Draw your own version beside theirs if you like, without comparing the two.
Stop when they put the pencil down, then look at the drawing together.

Choose a sturdy cup or soft fruit, and avoid glass or anything sharp on the table.

Use a jumbo crayon, a thick marker or a pencil wrapped in tape, and draw large shapes with the whole arm rather than small details.

activities.title: Sort a box of postcards
activities.summary: Look through a box of postcards or picture cards together and sort them into piles the person chooses.
steps: Look through the box first and set aside any card with writing you would rather not read aloud.
Place the box on the table and let them take out a card whenever they like.
Look at the card together and say what you can see, such as a beach, a flower or a bridge.
Offer a plate and ask whether they would like the card on a pile of its own or with another.
Let them choose the piles, such as places, colors or the ones they like best.
Move the card to the pile they choose, and move it again if they change their mind.
Carry on for as long as they enjoy it, and look at a favorite card for a while if they wish.
Put the piles back in the box in any order, or leave a favorite card on the table.

Keep the box small, so the pile never feels like a task to finish. Stop whenever they lose interest.
activities.stopNote: It is fine to stop after one card. Close the box, leave a favorite card where they can see it, and sit together for a while.

The child hands over one card at a time and the older adult decides which pile it joins. They can swap roles whenever they like.
Use a shallow tray or a large flat box lid, so the cards can be pushed across with the flat hand. Ask the helper to lift each card from the box and set it down in front of the person.

activities.title: Sort buttons by color
activities.summary: Sort a bowl of large buttons into a muffin tin or small dishes by color or size, in any order.
steps: Sit at a table with the bowl of buttons, the muffin tin and the tray in reach.
Pour a small handful of buttons onto the tray.
Pick up one button and look at its color and size.
Place it in a muffin cup or dish that matches, or start a new one.
Keep going, one button at a time, in whatever order they like.
Ask what they notice about the colors or sizes as the dishes fill up.
Tip the buttons back into the bowl, one dish at a time.
plainSteps: Sit at the table with the bowl of buttons.
Set the muffin tin and the tray within reach.
Pour a small handful of buttons onto the tray.
Pick up one button.
Look at its color and size.
Place it in a matching dish, or start a new one.
Keep going, one button at a time.
Ask what they notice about the colors or sizes.
Tip the buttons back into the bowl, one dish at a time.
materials: A bowl or tub of large buttons, in a few colors or sizes
A muffin tin, or a few small dishes or bowls
A tray or towel to work on
safety: Use only large buttons that cannot fit in the mouth, and remove any small or loose parts from the bowl.
Never use this with someone who puts things in their mouth. Stay close and keep the bowl on the table.
Count the buttons out at the start and back in at the end, so none are left on the floor or in a chair.
Check buttons for cracks, sharp edges or loose threads before use, and remove any that are damaged.
activities.stopNote: It is fine to stop after a few buttons. Tip the sorted buttons back into the bowl, and leave the dishes out for another time.

variations.text: The helper pre-sorts two or three colors into dishes, and the person adds one button at a time to the right one.
Use only smooth, plain buttons in two colors, and sort on a soft cloth instead of a hard tray.
Use dark dishes for pale buttons, or pale dishes for dark ones, so each button stands out against the dish.
Use only large, flat buttons, and sweep each one into its dish with the whole hand instead of picking up one at a time.

activities.title: Start a family recipe book
activities.summary: Talk about favorite dishes and write them down together, one page at a time.
steps: Sit together at a table with the notebook open to a blank page.
Ask about a dish they liked to make or eat, such as a Sunday meal or a holiday treat.
Write the name of the dish at the top of the page.
Ask what went into it and write the ingredients as a simple list. Rough amounts are fine.
Ask how it was made and write the steps in their own words.
Invite a story, such as who made it, where it was eaten, or what it smelled like.
Read the page back aloud and change anything they want changed.
Stop after one page, or carry on with another dish if you both want to.
plainSteps: Sit together at a table with the notebook.
Open it to a blank page.
Ask about a food they liked to make or eat.
For example, a Sunday meal or a holiday treat.
Write its name at the top of the page.
Ask what went into it.
Write the ingredients as a simple list.
Rough amounts are fine.
Ask how it was made.
Write the steps in their own words.
Invite a story about who made it.
Or about where it was eaten or what it smelled like.
Read the page back aloud.
Change anything they want changed.
Stop after one page.
Or carry on with another one if you both want to.
materials: A notebook, binder or a few sheets of lined paper
A pen that writes easily
Old recipe cards or cookbooks, if you have them
A few pictures of food from magazines or packaging (optional)
A folder or envelope to keep loose pages together
safety: This is a writing and talking activity, not cooking. Keep it away from a hot stove or oven, and do not test recipes during the session.
Food memories can bring up people who have died or hard times. Pause, listen, and let them lead, or move to another dish.
There are no wrong answers. If amounts or steps sound unusual, write them as told rather than correcting them.
If you later cook a recipe together, check for allergies, swallowing needs and diet advice first.
activities.stopNote: It is fine to stop after a single dish name. Close the book, leave it somewhere easy to find, and offer to add another page on a different day.

variations.text: Choose the dish together from two or three food pictures, and write only the name and one sentence about it.
A grandchild writes or types while the older adult tells the recipe. The child can draw the dish beside it.
Each person shares one dish. Collect the pages into a shared group book and make a copy for everyone.
Write in large, dark letters on unlined paper, one ingredient per line, and read each line aloud as you go.
Show pictures of foods and let them point to favorites. Write down what they chose, in their own book.
Use a thick marker or a pen wrapped in tape, and a large notebook that lies flat, so it does not need holding open.

activities.title: Tap a rhythm together
activities.summary: Tap along to a steady song on a table or small drum, taking turns to lead the beat.
steps: Sit where you can both reach the table or tray, with any drum or blocks in front of you.
Choose a song with a steady beat and play it at a comfortable volume.
Listen for a few bars and find the beat together.
Tap the beat gently, with one finger or a flat palm, at a speed that feels comfortable.
Invite them to tap along, copying what you do.
Swap places, so they lead and you copy the tap they choose.
Pause the song whenever they want a rest, and start again when they are ready.
Finish with one last tap together, then rest both hands on the table.
plainSteps: Sit where you can both reach the table or tray.
Keep any drum or blocks in front of you.
Choose a song with a steady beat.
Play it at a comfortable volume.
Listen for a few bars.
Find the beat together.
Tap the beat gently, with one finger or a flat palm.
Go at a speed that feels comfortable.
Invite them to tap along, copying what you do.
Swap places, so they lead.
Copy the tap they choose.
Pause the song whenever they want a rest.
Start again when they are ready.
Finish with one last tap together.
Then rest both hands on the table.
materials: A song with a clear, steady beat, saved on a phone or player
A table, a tray or the arm of a chair to tap on
A small hand drum, tambourine or pair of wooden blocks, if you have them
A folded towel or cushion to rest the arm on, if needed
safety: Keep taps gentle and stop if the hands or wrists hurt. Offer a softer surface or a slower song instead.
Use soft drumsticks, fingers or a flat palm. Hard sticks can bruise thin skin.
Keep the volume comfortable and check hearing aids are in and working. Loud bass can startle.
Small blocks can be swallowed. Keep them on the table or tray, and put them away when the activity ends.
Stay close while small blocks or drums are in use, and put them away when the activity ends.
activities.stopNote: It is fine to stop after a few bars. Rest the hands on the table, say that is enough for now, and sit quietly together.

variations.text: Let the helper tap the beat while the person listens, and join in with one finger or a single tap whenever they like.
Rest the hand on a pillow or blanket and tap softly. Keep the song low and short, a few minutes at a time.
Choose a soft, gentle song and tap with a flat hand rather than a drum. Keep the room quiet and the volume low.
A child leads with quick taps on a drum and the older adult follows, then the roles swap so each takes a turn.
Tap with a flat palm, or hold one large soft block or a wide hand drum in both hands so there is nothing small to grip.

activities.title: Make a torn paper mosaic
activities.summary: A picture built from small pieces of torn colored paper, with no scissors and no right way to place them.
steps: Draw a large, simple shape on the card together, such as a leaf, a house, a fish or a circle.
Tear a few pages into strips, then into pieces about the size of a postage stamp.
Sort the pieces into bowls by color, or leave them mixed if you both prefer.
Rub glue over a small part of the shape.
Press pieces onto the glued area, taking turns or working side by side.
Talk about the colors as you go, such as which ones remind you of a garden, the sea or a favorite coat.
Glue the next small area and keep filling the shape until it feels finished.
Leave it flat to dry and choose a place to show it.
plainSteps: Draw a large, simple shape on the card together.
Try a house, a fish or a circle.
Tear a few pages into strips.
Then tear the strips into pieces about the size of a postage stamp.
Sort the pieces into bowls by color.
Or leave them mixed if you both prefer.
Rub glue over a small part of the shape.
Press pieces onto the glued area.
Take turns, or work side by side.
Talk about the colors as you go.
Ask which ones remind you of the sea or a favorite coat.
Glue the next small area.
Keep filling the shape until it feels finished.
Leave it flat to dry.
Choose a place to show it.
materials: Colored paper, old magazine pages or wrapping paper
A sheet of card, about letter size
A glue stick
A pencil for the outline
Two or three shallow bowls or saucers to sort the pieces
safety: Keep small torn pieces away from anyone who may put paper in their mouth, and clear them away afterward.
Use a glue stick rather than liquid glue; check for skin sensitivity first.
Glossy magazine edges can occasionally nick skin, so offer softer paper if that is a concern.
Supervise closely while small torn pieces are on the table, and clear them away afterward.
activities.stopNote: It is fine to stop when only part of the shape is filled. A half-finished mosaic still looks good, and you can add more another day or leave it as it is.

variations.text: Tear all the pieces in advance and offer one bowl of a single color at a time.
Work on a lap tray with a raised edge so the pieces do not slide off.
Skip the tearing if the sound or feel is unpleasant, and use a small set of quiet, muted colors.
One person tears and hands over pieces while the other places them, then swap roles if they like.
Use a bold, thick outline on pale card and strongly contrasting colors, such as dark blue on yellow.
A child tears and sorts the pieces by color while the grandparent chooses where each one goes. Small pieces stay on the table.

activities.title: Thread a large bead bracelet
activities.summary: Slide large beads onto stretchy cord, one at a time, to make a simple bracelet to wear or give.
steps: Before you start, the helper cuts the elastic cord to about 12 inches and ties a knot in one end.
Wrap a short piece of clear tape around the other end to make a stiff tip for threading.
Place the beads in the tray, inside the raised edges, and sit with the tray in front of you.
Take one bead at a time and slide it onto the taped end of the cord.
Keep going until the bracelet is long enough to go around the wrist, leaving a few inches free.
Hold the cord firmly and tie a knot at the free end, so no bead can slide off.
The helper trims the extra cord with the scissors.
Put the beads back in the tray, counting them as you go.
plainSteps: Before you start, the helper cuts the cord to about 12 inches.
The helper ties a knot in one end.
Wrap clear tape around the other end.
Put the beads in the tray.
Take one bead at a time.
Slide it onto the taped end of the cord.
Keep going until the bracelet fits your wrist.
Leave a few inches of cord free.
Hold the cord firmly.
Tie a knot at the free end.
The helper trims the extra cord with the scissors.
Count the beads back into the tray.
materials: Large beads with big holes, enough for the bracelet
Stretchy elastic bead cord, about 12 inches long
Clear tape to stiffen one end of the cord
Scissors for the helper only
A tray with raised edges
safety: Beads and small pieces are a choking hazard for children under three and for anyone who mouths things. Do not use beads with an under-three or with anyone who mouths objects.
Use large beads only after the person's safety has been considered. Keep loose beads in the tray, and count them out and back in.
Elastic cord can snap back. Tie the knot before you let go, and keep the cord away from the face and eyes.
Do not use resin or epoxy to hold or seal beads. The fumes and skin contact are a hazard.
Scissors are for the helper only.
An adult stays nearby while beads are in use, and a finished bracelet is never worn on the neck.
activities.stopNote: It is fine to stop with a few beads on the cord. Tie a knot, put the beads back in the tray and count them, and finish another day, or leave it as it is.

variations.text: The helper ties the first knot and tapes the end, so the person only slides on the beads and says when to stop.
Sit at a table with the tray in front of you, and rest your forearms on the table while you thread.
Use a dark cord with pale beads, or the reverse, and lay the beads on a plain dark mat so each one shows.
Use beads with the biggest holes you can find, and thread with the whole hand rather than the fingertips.
Each person threads a bracelet from the same tray, and the group compares the finished bracelets at the end.

activities.title: Watch birds from a window
activities.summary: Sit by a window together, watch for birds, and describe their colors and how they move.
steps: Settle into a chair or bed by the window, with a blanket and a drink within reach.
Ask what they can see outside, or invite them to look for birds for a minute.
Wait quietly until a bird lands or flies past.
Ask what color the bird is, or what it is doing.
Trace the bird's path in the air with one finger, slowly, as it moves.
Draw a simple shape of the bird on the paper, using the color they name.
Listen for calls or song, and talk about how they sound.
Close the curtain if the glare is strong, and stop when they are ready.
plainSteps: Settle into a chair or bed by the window.

Ask what they can see outside.
Or invite them to look for birds for a minute.
Wait quietly until a bird lands or flies past.
Ask what color the bird is.
Or what it is doing.
Trace the bird's path in the air with one finger.
Move slowly, as the bird moves.
Draw a simple shape of the bird on the paper.

materials: A comfortable chair or bed positioned by a window with a view outside
A blanket or shawl for the lap
A sheet of paper and a few colored pencils or crayons
Binoculars or a magnifier, if they enjoy them
Optional: a bird feeder or bowl of water in view of the window
safety: Window glare can be strong. Use a sheer curtain or move the chair so the sun is not in the eyes.
Glass can be cold in winter or hot in summer. Keep a blanket on the lap and the room at a comfortable temperature.
Keep the window closed or fitted with a safety stop. Never let anyone lean out to see a bird.
Check glasses are clean and on before watching, so details are easier to see.
activities.stopNote: It is fine to stop when the birds leave. Close the curtain, sit quietly together, and try again on another day.

variations.text: Use a ready-made chart with simple bird shapes to color in. The only jobs are choosing colors and pointing out the birds.
Prop pillows behind them so they can see the window from bed. Keep the watch short, ten minutes or less, and rest between birds.
Use bold colored markers on large paper and describe the birds' size and movement aloud. Bring the chair closer to the window.
A child draws the birds on the paper while the older adult describes their colors and how they move.
Use jumbo crayons to draw, and rest the binoculars on a folded blanket on the lap so they do not need to be held up.

activities.title: Weave paper strips
activities.summary: Weave colored paper strips over and under a card base that the helper has already slit.
steps: Lay the slit card on the table, with the slits running up and down and the strips within reach.
Choose the first strip together. Any color is fine.
Start at the bottom and push the strip over the first upright strip of card, then under the next, and so on across.
Pull the strip gently so it lies flat, but not so tight that the card bends.
For the next row, start the opposite way: under the first upright, then over the next.
Push each new row up against the last one, so the card is covered.
When a strip runs out, tape its end to the back of the card and start a new strip.
Stop when the card is covered, then tape down the loose ends on the back.
plainSteps: Lay the slit card on the table, slits running up and down.
Keep the strips within reach.
Choose the first strip together.
Any color is fine.
Start at the bottom and push the strip over the first upright.
Push it under the next, and so on across.
Pull gently, so the strip lies flat without bending the card.
For the next row, go under the first upright, then over the next.
Push each new row up against the last one.
When a strip runs out, tape its end to the back.
Start a new strip.
Stop when the card is covered.
Tape down the loose ends on the back.
materials: A sheet of thick card, about letter size, with parallel slits cut by the helper about one inch apart, stopping one inch short of the top and bottom edges
Colored paper or thin card in two or three colors, cut by the helper into strips about one inch wide
Scissors and a ruler for the helper
A glue stick or low-tack tape
safety: Scissors are for the helper only. The person weaves with their hands alone.
Check the slit edges for sharp corners, and round them off with the helper before weaving.
Use a glue stick or low-tack tape, and keep small pieces away from the mouth.
activities.stopNote: It is fine to stop after one row. Leave the card on the table with the strips in place, and carry on another time, or just enjoy the colors.

variations.text: Weave with one color and wide strips, and work only the middle row together.
Use a clipboard on a lap tray, with the strips already cut and a few rows woven together.
Use high-contrast strips on a dark card base, and describe each over and under aloud.
Place a strip in their hand and guide it gently over and under, pausing to see if they want to go on.
A child cuts the strips in advance, and the two take turns on each row.
Use wide, stiff strips that can be pushed over and under with the flat hand, so no pinch grip is needed.

activities.title: Wind a ball of yarn
activities.summary: Wind a skein or tangle of yarn into a neat ball together, taking turns holding and winding.
steps: Sit facing each other or side by side, with the yarn between you.
Ask if they would prefer to hold the yarn or wind it.
Find the loose end of the yarn together.
Wrap the end around two fingers a few times to start the ball.
Slide it off your fingers and keep winding around that small bundle.
Turn the ball a little every few wraps so it stays round.
Swap jobs whenever either of you would like to.
Tuck the end under the last wrap and drop the ball in the bowl.
plainSteps: Sit with the yarn between you.
Ask whether they would like to hold or wind.
Find the loose end of the yarn together.
Wrap the end around two fingers a few times.
Slide the bundle off your fingers.
Keep winding around that small bundle.
Turn the ball a little every few wraps.
Swap jobs whenever either of you likes.
Tuck the end under the last wrap.
Drop the finished ball in the bowl.
materials: A skein or loose length of soft, chunky yarn
A small bowl or basket for the finished ball
safety: Loose yarn is a trip and tangle hazard. Keep it in a basket and gather it up before anyone stands or walks.
Never wrap yarn around a wrist, finger or neck tightly enough to press, and keep long strands away from the neck.
Choose soft yarn that does not shed fibers; some wool can itch or irritate sensitive skin.
Put the yarn away when the activity ends so nobody catches a foot in it later.
activities.stopNote: It is fine to stop with a small ball and plenty of yarn left. Put it all in the basket together and pick it up again another day, or not at all.

variations.text: Start the ball beforehand around a cardboard tube. The only job is turning the tube slowly while the helper feeds the yarn.
Rest the ball on a tray or pillow and keep the loose yarn in a basket on the lap. Wind for a few minutes at a time.
Choose smooth cotton yarn in a single soft color instead of fluffy or brightly variegated yarn.
Use thick yarn in a strong color against a plain dark lap blanket so the strand is easy to follow.
A child holds the skein on outstretched hands while the older adult winds, or the other way around.
Wind around a wide cardboard tube held in the whole hand, not two fingers, and let the helper steady the skein on a chair back.

activities.title: Wrap a small gift
activities.summary: Wrap a small, unbreakable gift together for someone they choose, then tie it up and add a tag.
steps: Ask who the gift is for and place it on the table in front of them.
Lay out the paper and ask whether they would like to choose a plain or a patterned sheet.
Set the gift in the middle of the paper and fold one side over it.
Bring the other side across and hold it while the helper puts on a piece of tape.
Fold in the two ends and tape them down, one at a time.
Lay the ribbon around the parcel and tie it, or let the helper tie it while they hold the ribbon.
Write the tag together, or let them mark it with a name or a drawing, and tie it on.
Put the finished gift somewhere safe and agree together when to give it.
plainSteps: Ask who the gift is for.
Place the gift on the table in front of them.
Lay out the paper.
Ask whether they would like a plain or patterned sheet.
Set the gift in the middle of the paper.
Fold one side over it.
Bring the other side across.
Hold it while the helper puts on a piece of tape.
Fold in the two ends.
Tape them down, one at a time.
Lay the ribbon around the parcel.
Tie it, or let the helper tie it while they hold the ribbon.
Write the tag together, or let them mark it with a name or drawing.
Tie the tag on.
Put the finished gift somewhere safe.
Agree together when to give it.
materials: A small, unbreakable gift, such as a book or a soft scarf
Wrapping paper, or plain paper or a clean cloth
Ribbon or string, cut in short lengths
Tape
Scissors, kept by the helper
A gift tag or a small piece of card, and a thick pen
safety: Keep the scissors with the helper. Cut the paper, tape and ribbon before you start.
Tape can be hard to peel for some hands and can tug on skin. Stick strips to the edge of the table ready to pick up.
Choose a gift that cannot break and has nothing loose that could come off. A book, a scarf or a pack of cards works well.
Use ribbon in short lengths and take it away at the end. Do not leave loose lengths within reach.
activities.stopNote: It is fine to stop at any point. Leave the gift half wrapped, or put it in a bag as it is. The thought of giving is the main part.

variations.text: The helper wraps the gift in paper beforehand, and the person chooses the ribbon, ties it on and adds the tag.
Set a firm tray across the lap or on a bed table, with the paper, the gift and pre-cut tape strips on it. Work on one fold at a time.
Use a thick ribbon or a wide strip of cloth that is easy to hold. Put tape strips along the edge of the tray so they are ready to pick up.
Two people each hold a side of the paper, fold together, and take turns with the tape and the ribbon.
The older adult decides how to fold and where the ribbon goes, and the child holds the paper and hands over tape strips. Scissors stay with an adult.

activities.title: Write a letter together
activities.summary: Write a short letter or postcard together, with the helper writing as the person says what to put.
steps: Sit side by side at a table with the paper, the pen and the envelope in reach.
Ask who the letter is for and what they would like to say. Any answer is the right one.
Write the greeting at the top, in the words the person chooses.
Ask one open question, such as what has been on their mind this week, and write down the answer.
Read the sentences back aloud and ask if they want to change anything.
Add a drawing, or tape a pressed flower to a corner.
Sign the letter together, then fold it.
Put the letter in the envelope, write the address and add a stamp, or set it aside to give in person.
plainSteps: Sit side by side at a table.

Write the greeting at the top, in the words they choose.
Ask one open question.
For example, what has been on their mind this week.

Write the address and add a stamp.
Or set it aside to give in person.
materials: A sheet of notepaper or a plain postcard
A pen or pencil that is easy to grip
An envelope and stamp, if the letter will be posted
Optional: a pressed flower and a little tape, or a pencil for a small drawing
safety: Never write bank details, passwords or PINs in a letter. Check the address before sealing the envelope.
Keep pens and stamps away from the mouth if the person may chew or taste things.
Check before adding a flower; some plants can cause skin irritation or allergy.
activities.stopNote: It is fine to stop after one sentence. Put the letter aside, and finish it another day, or simply talk about the person it is for.

variations.text: Offer one or two ready-made openings to choose from, such as Thinking of you or Hope you are well.
Use a clipboard on a lap tray, and keep the letter to one short paragraph.
Offer two options for each line and write the one the person nods at or points to.
Use a dark felt-tip marker on large, plain paper, and read each line aloud as you write it.
A child writes the greeting and adds a drawing while the older adult says what to put in the letter.
Use a thick marker or a pen wrapped in a foam hair curler, and write a short greeting. The helper can write the rest.
